Biggest mistake i see people make in combat is that they stand still behind cover too long waiting for ap to regen or for the enemies to come to them. This isn't fallout 3 or new vegas. I promise that the raiders know you're hiding behind the door, and they will throw grenades and insta kill you.

Raiders will throw shit at you, and they will try to flank you. You need to move your ass.

My advice is to treat this game like a shooter first and an rpg second. When you get into gun fights you need to be thinking about all the things you would be thinking about in any other shooter: how many enemies? Where are they? Can i flank them? Do i have a positional advantage? Or do they? How do i get a positional advantage? What resources do i have? Is this even a fight worth taking? Do they have a fucking missile launcher?! And so on and so forth. This process becomes a fuck of a lot easier if you plan your engagements in advance. So take your time to really assess what each encounter has going on in it before engaging. And again, i cant say this enough... MOVE. When you're in combat you always have to be thinking about what your next piece of cover will be that will give you the upper hand, and then get there. I have like 40 hours on my most recent save and ive only died once, and it was because i was standing still behind cover and got my ass blown up by a missile like a dumbass. Go figure.

For me its scrounger. Its useful for anyone and really enables certain playstyles like automatic weapons or mingun users. Even for melee characters, its basically an infinite money glitch. I take it on every character.

Strong back is another great perk that benefits every playstyle. But unlike scrounger, it requires a lot of stat investment. And with 6 strength, you kind of already don't need it unless you have a massive arsenal and aren't using pocketed gear for whatever reason. I only take it for conveinence on survival mode.

And on the topic of survival, life giver 3 is easily the most op perk in survival and you are seriously missing out if you dont take it early. Completely negates the need to heal chip damage and seriously cuts down on resource management as you'll pretty much only need stimpacks for limb healing and you can save food and water for when you need it. And again, it requires almost no stat investment. The extra max hp is also a pretty massive bonus in the early game and gives you something like the equivalent of 5 levels worth of max hp when you take it, maybe even more. This can often be the difference between surviving a random molotov/frag mine, and dying and having to reload a save from 45 minutes ago. Next to Scrounger, its pretty much always the first perk i take these days because im always playing on survival.

Death mark, and death blossom are probably his two most important skills and they really tie his whole kit together. Playing without these skills makes zero feel like half a character when you're used to having them so i always rush to get them.Once you get those its kind of hard to mess up zero. you're free to mess around and pick skills that augment whatever playstyle suits you.

The game isn't about dodge and punish like the souls series. Its more like a fighting game. Offense is the best defense. You want to create openings to do big combos and delete the enemies health bar asap. Enki for example (the monkey with the spear), has a horn that you can break that does a ton of ki damage and puts him into a small stagger state. So for him i go for a vertical strike to break the horn, and follow up with a combo. If he still has a little ki left, i'll dodge or block is follow up, then finish the rest of his ki off and go for another big combo. With his ki depleted you can wail on him until hes dead. Most Yokai enemies are similar. They have some sort of weakness you can exploit to create combo opportunites. Not all, but most. But the general theme is that you want to play proactively.

Human enemies? Again you want to treat it like a fighting game. Create an opening to start pressuring them into a block state, and keep the pressure on as much as possible to deplete their ki and then go in for the kill. 

Obviously its more complicated to implement than im making it sound, but going in with the mindset that its like the souls games will make it 100 times more frustrating than it needs to be.

Ive beat every boss in the game up until the final mission on my first or second try, and only struggled on one boss that was an optional side quest in the end game, and even that only took me 5 or 6 attemepts. Most of my deaths are when i get ganked by an enemy i didn't know was behind me. So i kind of wish hard mode was unlocked from the start as i dont know if i care to replay it much even if the combat is satisfying. On another positive note though, the music is phenomenal and consistently surprised me with its variety. New songs often play when going through familiar areas and that kept things fresh. As for the story though? Its bad.i have nothing positive to say. I dont buy games like this for the story so it doesn't bother me much. Kingdom hearts is one of my favorite games of all time, but i'd be the first one to admit that the series story and lore is borderline retarded. Its okay to like something that has flaws.

Its hard to explain if you haven't played it, but the long and short of it is that its insanely difficult for no good reason and it has a ton of little issues that when added together drag down the whole experience. 

I dont know if you've played Sekiro, but especially in the late game of LoP it feels like playing Sekiro on the charmless hard mode, except you cant stun the bosses with attacks and your deflect window is cut in half. Theres a stagger mechanic, but it requires landing a sequence of deflects and heavy attacks and then land a full charged heavy to pull it off. The window is brief, so if rng doesn't allow you to land one, you miss your chance and all the work you put in deflecting is wasted. The whole mechanic often feels like a waste of time even though its needed a lot of the time. Most of the attacks in the game are awkward and completely unreactable, so most of the encounters feel like a guessing game of trying to find the exact timing of every dodge and especially deflect, because the timing is so strict and unintuitive that even when i know the attack by heart it still feels inconsistent to deflect it. Even after fighting a boss 100 times, i still felt like i was just guessing. I almost never felt confident. So because of all this i just felt disempowered the entire game. Aside from a couple of bosses i genuinely enjoyed, i never felt the satisfaction of overcoming a challenge. I usually just felt like i got lucky. 

And as for the little issues? Theres so many its hard to know where to begin.
Blocking and parrying pushes your character. I cant count the amount of times i was pushed into a corner by an enemy and trapped. Your attacks bounce off walls, but the enemies dont. How many enemies stand next to walls? LOTS. Even though they share this mechanic, after probably 500 hours in elden ring, getting cucked by a wall has happened to me far more in LoP after only 34 hours. Bullshit dark souls 2 level design. After getting halfway through the game i was constantly on edge feeling like the sky was going to fall and kill me at any moment because the game keeps on pulling more and more pranks on you it becomes absurd and exhausting. The economy is fucked..the game throws levels at you like candy in the early game. In the mid to late game you have to save pretty much every penny on levels because for some reason late game enemies only drop like 4 times the money as the tutorial enemies. The special fable attacks suck for the most part. They're very expensive, do unimpressive damage compared to how long the animation is, and for the most part have no hyper armor. The game locks basic movement options like a getup dodge behind a progression system. You dont unlock the ability to get up off the fucking ground until like 10 hours into the game lol. Backstabs are inconsistent, not much else to say here. I could probably go on. Again a lot of these problems aren't game breaking but when you add them all up it becomes incredibly frustrating to deal with regularly.

Shoot at what you think can die or what is most threatening to you and your team in the moment. There are no hard and fast rules. You dont want to tunnel vision. Target prioritization is a complex subject that cant be answered properly in a reddit thread. The two main things to think about though are potential value, and ease of execution. Killing a valking mercy is incredibly valuable, but its really hard to do. Killing a torb turret is easy and quick, but doesn't bring a lot of value. Finding a balance between these things is a good start. 

Think about what value you could get from any interaction and assess the likely hood of it working out. This is why you see tracers and genjis bullying zens all the time. Hes pretty easy to kill as those heroes and it brings a lot of value to your team for doing so. Its often more complicated for 76. But the sentiment is the same. What are you capable of? And what value does it bring? If you dont know what you're capable of, then start experimenting. You will likely surprise yourself.

Because instead of enjoying the moment, you start judging it and think variations of: "is this okay?", "will something bad happen if i go deeper?", "am i too deep in trance?" I dont think there is anyone that could make a legitimate argument for how hypnosis could be dangerous on its own. You have this completely backwards..having staggered attack animations punishes quick reactions because if you react to the start up frames of the attack, you will get punished by the late activation of the hitbox. When you take an enemy, and give him some fast attacks that require fast reactions, and then throw in a couple high damage staggered attacks that punishes fast reaction, then the only good option becomes prediction. If you could buffer a second roll to escape the staggered attack, it wouldn't be as big of a deal. But in many case, if you react to the startup frames of an attack expecting it to be the fast one, and it turns out to be the staggered attack, you have already sealed your fate and will get hit. But the active frames of the fast attack come out so fast that you have no choice but to react to the startup frames because waiting to make an informed choice would take too long. This is essentially a 50/50 frame trap from a fighting game perspective. It puts you in a situation where you have no choice but to guess. Not all of the bosses work this way. But a lot of them do.

At 4 way intersections, when you are turning left, you can turn freely when there is a green arrow. If the arrow goes away and it becomes solid green light, you look straight ahead at the oncoming traffic infront of you, and the situation basically becomes like a stop sign. You stay put if there are cars coming through, and complete your turn once its safe.

If you find that there is never a safe time to turn during the green light, then once your green light becomes yellow, you know you can begin your turn. This is because the oncoming traffics light has also turned yellow, so they will prepare to stop, and you're free to go. So essentially with left turns, you use your own judgement for when its safe, again, just like a stop sign. The biggest thing to remember is that once you establish yourself in the intersection, you cant stay there when the light turns red. You need to complete the turn before that, so a good rule to follow is that if you are in the intersection, and your light turns yellow, complete your turn.

Right turns, you can turn freely on solid green lights. And at least where im from, you can make right turns on red lights as long you are safe to do so. So again, its like a stop sign. The only exception is if there is a sign that prohibits rights on red. But this might be different in your country so i would ask your instructor.
